title: SQL adherence
text:
Why does Qwen’s SQL fail to run, and what fixes it? Fix in code what code can fix safely, and spend a model call only on what is left. cut keeps the reply’s SQL up to the first semicolon that ends a complete statement (sqlglot finds it, so a ; inside a string survives) and never rewrites the query. pydantic checks the SQL (one SELECT, known columns, DuckDB’s EXPLAIN) and sends its error back for one retry. json is the provider’s strict JSON-schema mode. 12 questions x 3 epochs per model and variant.
Post-processing, case by case (every change is in repairs.jsonl). The sqlglot cut: 9 answers cut, 9 of them then correct, none changed in meaning. Rewrite: 3 answers, 2 then correct. It quotes a reserved alias (JOIN zones do becomes JOIN zones AS "do"). The first post-processing, with its plain split at ;, ran 3 repaired answers to a wrong value. In q08 it dropped a stray 0, and a wrong query that would have failed returned 100 against 14.81: an error became a confident wrong number.
Not tried: GEPA prompt optimization in DSPy, set aside on purpose: it needs its own held-out training questions (a later lecture or a project option).

We ran each eval block once. Each block holds 36 answers (12 questions, 3 times each), but a proper statistical comparison would need several independent runs of every variant and a paired comparison on the same questions, reported with a confidence interval rather than a single percentage.

With strict JSON mode on, Qwen often ends a correct query with the end of the JSON (;"}, ;,). The cut removes it in code, so the validator sends 5 retries instead of 13, for 40% less. Every cut answer passed. When JSON mode is off, Qwen does not write that junk, so the cut finds nothing to do. Cut alone on the json run’s replies: 6 cuts, SQL errors 28% → 11%. GPT-5.4 nano and mini: 0% SQL errors with the validator, in every variant.

title: SQL adherence
text:
One failure, traced
q08 “What percentage of all trips were paid in cash?” on Qwen, pydantic. The first reply makes 2 temp tables before its SELECT. The validator answers: the SQL holds 3 statements: send exactly one SELECT, with no comments or text before or after it. The retry sends one SELECT, and DuckDB returns 14.81, the reference.

title: Guardrails
text: What does the app do when someone attacks it? 20 attacks (evals/guardrails/redteam.yml) and 12 real questions (benign.yml) go through the app with four guard settings. The input guard reads the question before the model sees it (a pattern rule, or a classifier model). The output guard parses the model’s SQL and allows one read-only query over the two tables. DuckDB is opened read-only in every setting.

The rule stops the phrasings it has patterns for and misses their paraphrases. The classifier stops almost every direct attack, for one extra model call per question. Neither input guard can see an indirect injection (r18 to r20): the question is harmless, and the instruction arrives in the data or in the retrieved text. Every statement that reached DuckDB in the guarded settings had passed the output guard, so it was one read-only query over the two tables.

title: Correctness
text: Does the app answer correctly? Each model answers 12 questions about the taxi table 3 times. An answer passes three checks: its reply fits the schema, its SQL runs in DuckDB, and DuckDB’s number matches the reference SQL’s number. Counts must match exactly, averages and percentages within 1%.

We ran each eval block once. Each block holds 36 answers (12 questions, 3 times each), but a proper statistical comparison would need several independent runs of every variant and a paired comparison on the same questions, reported with a confidence interval rather than a single percentage.

Most failures are on q12, “What is the average trip length?”. The question does not say minutes or miles. The reference reads it as minutes. 7 of 9 answers read it as miles, with high confidence and a query that runs. Only the value check catches them.
One vocabulary line in the data description (“trip length” means the duration in minutes) fixes it for the GPT models. Passes on q12 after the fix: Qwen 3.8 27B 2 of 3, GPT-5.4 nano 3 of 3, GPT-5.4 mini 3 of 3.

The querychat question is the notebook’s “What is the average tip by payment type?”, asked once per model. Every call resends the system prompt, so input tokens dominate. OpenAI bills the repeated start of the prompt at the cached price. Groq lists no cached price for Qwen. The eval answers in one call with no tool loop, so each answer is cheaper.
Guards: the input rule and the output guard add nothing to the bill. The input classifier adds about $0.10 per 1,000 questions.

title: Taxi questions: evals
text:
An analyst asks a question about a month of New York taxi trips in plain words. A language model writes the SQL, guards check the question and the query, and DuckDB computes the answer. These pages report how well that app answers, what its guards stop and what it costs to run.
